docs.title: C-style
docs.text: C-style interfaces are generally preferred with a few supporting types. The simpler C-style interface leads to less intermediate code that the compiler needs to work with and it increases the likelihood that functions will be inlined. Inlining is a critical and integral part of performance for any math library. In general, code commonly used and that would benefit the most from being inlined uses a C-style API (vectors, quaternions, etc) while less critical code relies on various helper types (angles, helpers, etc).

docs.title: C++11
docs.text:
We restrict the code to use C++11 as it is the most widely used flavor on the platforms we currently support. constexpr in particular is used as much as possible. Despite the C-style API, everything lives under the rtm namespace and implementation details not meant to be consumed by clients is hidden inside the rtm_impl namespace as well as the impl header directory.

The library is 100% comprised of C++ headers and no linking is required. This makes for the easiest integration possible and it also gives us more freedom with what and when we can change things.

docs.title: Argument passing
docs.text:
This library supports many architectures, platforms, and compilers and sadly there is no consensus on how SIMD types should be passed by argument or returned by value. It is generally best to pass as many things by register, when possible, but usually only a certain number of registers can be used for it. Some platforms support aggregate types being passed by register (either by argument and/or by return value), others do not. To keep things as simple as possible, aliases are used for every type such as: vector4f_arg0, vector4f_arg1, ..., vector4f_argn.

RTM tries its best to do things optimally. Generally speaking, for code that isn't performance critical the difference will be very small and you are free to pass things by value or const& in your own code but using the argument aliases is encouraged.

docs.title: Matrix multiplication ordering
docs.text:
Whether you call it pre or post-multiplication, or left or right multiplication, it boils down to whether vectors are represented as rows or as columns.

In the former case, multiplication with a matrix takes the form v' = vM while in the later case we have v' = Mv. Linear algebra typically treats vectors as columns and OpenGL opted to use that convention for that reason. If you think of matrices as functions that modify an input and return an output it ends up reading like this: result = object_to_world(local_to_object(input)). This reads right-to-left as is common with nested function evaluation. Sadly, this somewhat breaks down when using multiplication operators: result = object_to_world * local_to_object * input. Regardless of how operator precedence works, the result will be identical but most modern programming languages (and western languages) read left-to-right.

On the other hand, DirectX uses row vectors and ends up with the much more natural: result = input * local_to_object * object_to_world. Your input is in local space, it gets transformed into object space before finally ending up in world space. Clean, clear, and readable. If you instead multiply the two matrices together on their own, you get the clear local_to_world = local_to_object * object_to_world instead of the awkward local_to_world = object_to_world * local_to_object you would get with OpenGL and column vectors.

An executive decision was made for all vectors to be row vectors for their improved readability.

docs.title: Coordinate frame
docs.text:
When relevant, a left-handed coordinate system is used:

  • X axis = forward
  • Y axis = right
  • Z axis = up

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: In order to contribute to RTM you will first need to setup your environment.

docs.title: Windows, Linux, and OS X for x86 and x64
docs.text:
1. Install CMake 3.2 or higher (3.14 for Visual Studio 2019, 4.2 for Visual Studio 2026, or 3.10 on OS X with Xcode 10), Python 2.7 or 3, and the proper compiler for your platform.
  2. Execute git submodule update --init to get the files of external submodules (e.g. Catch2).
  3. Generate the IDE solution with: python make.py The solution is generated under ./build
  4. Build the IDE solution with: python make.py -build
  5. Run the unit tests with: python make.py -unit_test
  6. Build and run benchmarks with the -bench switch
  7. Run the clang static analyzer on the public headers with: python make.py -analyze

On all three platforms, AVX support can be enabled by using the -avx switch and AVX2 with -avx2. Intrinsic usage can be turned off with -nosimd.

The -analyze switch runs the clang static analyzer on the include validation files, one file for each public header. It analyzes the functions in the headers and enables the array bound checker. It needs clang and a Makefile or Ninja generator: use the default compiler on OS X, or -compiler clang19 (or a later version) on Linux. It prints each issue one time and returns an error code if it finds an issue. On GitHub Actions, it also prints each issue as an annotation on the line of the issue. The other switches apply: for example, -nosimd analyzes the scalar code path.

docs.title: Linux riscv64
docs.text:
For native Linux on riscv64, the steps are identical to x86 and x64 and the generic scalar path is selected automatically. You can generate build files with: python make.py -cpu riscv64

Cross-compilation to riscv64 is not handled by make.py. Use CMake directly with a proper RISC-V compiler and toolchain file instead.

docs.title: Linux ARMv7
docs.text:
For native Linux on ARMv7, the steps are identical to x86 and x64 and make.py selects the armv7 architecture automatically. You can generate build files with: python make.py -cpu armv7

With SIMD enabled, the build adds -mfpu=neon because the Linux armhf compilers do not enable NEON by default.

docs.title: Windows ARM64
docs.text: For Windows on ARM64, the steps are identical to x86 and x64 but you will need CMake 3.13 or higher and you must provide the architecture on the command line: python make.py -compiler vs2017 -cpu arm64

docs.title: Windows ARM64EC
docs.text:
For Windows on ARM64EC, the steps are identical to Windows ARM64. ARM64EC needs Visual Studio 2019 or later. You must provide the architecture on the command line: python make.py -compiler vs2022 -cpu arm64ec

On an x64 host, make.py cross-compiles. It does not register the unit tests with CTest, thus -unit_test does not run them. To run the unit tests, use an ARM64 host.

docs.title: Android
docs.text:
For Android, the steps are identical to Windows, Linux, and OS X but you also need to install Android NDK 21 (or higher). Use -compiler android. The default architecture is arm64. Use -cpu armv7 for 32-bit ARM. Make sure that the adb executable is in your PATH. The -tests_matching switch is not supported on Android.

On Windows, the build uses gradle. The -unit_test and -bench switches install the app on the device and run it.

Android Studio v3.5 can be used to launch and debug. After running CMake to build and generate everything, the Android Studio projects can be found under the ./build directory.

Note that running the benchmark on Android can be done but it currently involves a number of manual steps.

On OS X and Linux, the build uses the CMake toolchain of the NDK. make.py finds the NDK with the ANDROID_NDK_HOME or ANDROID_NDK_ROOT environment variable. If neither is set, it uses the most recent version in the ndk directory of ANDROID_HOME or ANDROID_SDK_ROOT. The -unit_test switch copies the unit test executable to /data/local/tmp on the device with adb and runs it there. The output of the unit tests shows in the terminal, and make.py returns an error code if a test fails. Use the ANDROID_SERIAL environment variable to select a device when more than one is connected. The benchmark is not supported with this build.

For example, on OS X with Homebrew:

brew install --cask android-platform-tools android-ndk
export ANDROID_NDK_HOME="/opt/homebrew/share/android-ndk"
python3 make.py -compiler android -build -unit_test

docs.title: iOS
docs.text:
For iOS, the steps are identical to the other platforms but due to code signing, you will need to perform the builds from Xcode manually. Note that this is only an issue if you attempt to use the unit tests locally.

In order to run these manually:

  • Open the Xcode project for the appropriate tool
  • In the project settings, enable automatic code signing and select your development team
  • Build and run on your device

Note that iOS builds have never been tested on an emulator.

docs.title: Emscripten
docs.text:
Emscripten support currently only has been tested on OS X and Linux. To use it, make sure to install a recent version of Emscripten SDK 1.39.11+.

By default, make.py compiles the Emscripten unit tests with WebAssembly SIMD (-msimd128). To test the scalar code path, use -nosimd. The unit tests run with Node.js, which must support WebAssembly SIMD (version 16.4 or later).

docs.title: Commit message format
docs.text: This library uses the angular.js message format and it is enforced with commit linting through every pull request.

docs.title: Handling asserts
docs.text:
This library uses a simple system to handle asserts. Asserts are fatal and must terminate otherwise the behavior is undefined if execution continues.

A total of 4 behaviors are supported:

  • We can print to stderr and abort
  • We can throw and exception
  • We can call a custom function
  • Do nothing and strip the check at compile time (default behavior)

Everything necessary is implemented in rtm/impl/error.h.

Note: It is NOT possible to have different assert behaviors in two or more C++ object files. All the C++ files within your static or dynamic library that reference RTM must all use the same assert handling strategy.

docs.title: Aborting
docs.text:
In order to enable the aborting behavior, simply define the macro RTM_ON_ASSERT_ABORT:

#define RTM_ON_ASSERT_ABORT

docs.title: Throwing
docs.text:
In order to enable the throwing behavior, simply define the macro RTM_ON_ASSERT_THROW:

#define RTM_ON_ASSERT_THROW

Note that the type of the exception thrown is std::runtime_error.

docs.title: Custom function
docs.text:
In order to enable the custom function calling behavior, define the macro RTM_ON_ASSERT_CUSTOM with the name of the function to call:

#define RTM_ON_ASSERT_CUSTOM on_custom_assert_impl

Note that the function signature is as follow: void on_custom_assert_impl(const char* expression, int line, const char* file, const char* format, ...) {}

You can also define your own assert implementation by defining the RTM_ASSERT macro as well:

#define RTM_ON_ASSERT_CUSTOM
#define RTM_ASSERT(expression, format, ...) checkf(expression, ANSI_TO_TCHAR(format), #__VA_ARGS__)

docs.title: No checks
docs.text: By default if no macro mentioned above is defined, all asserts will be stripped at compile time.

docs.title: SIMD support
docs.text: RTM does not use the reciprocal estimate and the reciprocal square root estimate instructions (for example rcpps, rsqrtps, and vrecpe). The precision of these instructions is not the same on all CPUs. RTM uses a division and a square root instead. Modern CPUs hide most of the latency of the division and the square root, and the code has fewer instructions.

docs.title: x86 and x64
docs.text:
Various versions of SSE are supported: SSE2, SSE3, SSE4, AVX, AVX2, and FMA.

Note that even when FMA is enabled, its intrinsics are not used because they appear slower on at least Haswell and Ryzen.

docs.title: ARM
docs.text:
Both ARM NEON and ARM64 NEON are supported.

ARM64EC uses the ARM64 NEON code path. MSVC also defines _M_X64 for ARM64EC, but RTM does not use the SSE intrinsics there because ARM64EC emulates them. RTM does not use __vectorcall on ARM64EC.

docs.title: WebAssembly
docs.text:
WebAssembly SIMD128 is supported. To enable it, compile with -msimd128. Clang then defines __wasm_simd128__ and RTM defines RTM_WASM128_INTRINSICS. Without -msimd128, RTM uses the scalar code path.

  • The relaxed SIMD instructions are not used. Thus, the results do not change between the browsers and the CPUs.
  • vector_min and vector_max use the pmin and pmax instructions. They have the same semantics as std::min and std::max, and they compile to a single instruction on x64.

docs.title: Types supported
docs.text:
Realtime Math supports the most commonly used types in video games and realtime applications in a SIMD friendly way with a strong focus on performance.

All types come in various flavors with a corresponding suffix for their width (e.g. vector4f):

  • f for float32
  • d for float64
  • s for int16
  • i for int32
  • q for int64

docs.title: Scalar
docs.text: Both regular float & double types are supported for most operations and a special SIMD friendly scalar type as well: scalarf & scalard. Different architectures have an easier or harder time working with scalar floating point numbers. For example, older PowerPC processors had to write to memory and reload from it to transfer from one register file into another (e.g convert from a float to a SIMD vector). Modern processors handle this much better but inefficiencies remain, especially with SSE. While it is free to convert a SIMD scalar into a float with _mm_cvtss_f32(..) the reverse generally requires the compiler to fill the unused SIMD lanes with known values (either zero or the same). This introduces an extra instruction that isn't always required when only the first lane is used such as with scalar_sqrt_reciprocal(..). By introducing a type for SIMD scalar values, each platform is free to make an optimal choice.

docs.title: Vector 4D
docs.text:
Lower dimensions vectors will not be supported with proper types but functions can support them with an appropriate suffix (e.g. vector_dot3(..)). If no suffix is specified, functions operate on the full width of the vector. When a function operates on a reduced number of SIMD lanes, the extra unused lanes will have undefined values.

Vectors are row vectors in RTM and thus multiply on the left of matrices.

docs.title: Mask 4D
docs.text: A comparison mask used by vector selection/blending. Each SIMD lane consists of all ones (true) or zeroes (false) depending on the condition.

docs.title: Quaternion
docs.text: Quaternions are 4D complex numbers commonly used to represent 3D rotations (when normalized). The [xyz] components are the real part while the [w] component is the imaginary part.

docs.title: VQ (vector-quaternion)
docs.text:
A VQ represents an affine transform in two distinct parts: a rotation quaternion and a vector3 translation. This type is commonly used in video games as it is very fast to work with and more compact than a full affine matrix.

Before 2.4, the name of this type was QV. The new name follows the order of operations from right to left (rotation, translation), as in the literature.

docs.title: VQS (vector-quaternion-scalar)
docs.text:
A VQS represents an affine transform in three distinct parts: a rotation quaternion, a vector4 translation, and a scalar uniform scale. This type is commonly used in video games as it is very fast to work with and more compact than a full affine matrix. It represents uniform positive/negative scale through a single scalar value. When multiplying transforms of this type, scale combines as it would with matrices.

Before 2.4, the name of this type was QVS. The new name follows the order of operations from right to left (scale, rotation, translation), as in the literature.

docs.title: VQV (vector-quaternion-vector)
docs.text:
A VQV represents an affine transform in three distinct parts: a rotation quaternion, a vector3 translation, and a vector3 non-uniform scale. This type is commonly used in video games as it is very fast to work with and more compact than a full affine matrix. It properly handles positive non-uniform scaling but negative scaling is a bit more problematic. A best effort is made by converting the quaternion to a matrix when necessary. If scale fidelity is important, consider using VQM or an affine matrix 3x4 instead. When multiplying transforms of this type, scale combines as it would with matrices.

Before 2.4, the name of this type was QVV. The new name follows the order of operations from right to left (scale, rotation, translation), as VQS does in the literature.

docs.title: VQM (vector-quaternion-matrix)
docs.text:
A VQM represents an affine transform in three distinct parts: a rotation quaternion, a vector3 translation, and a 3x3 scale/shear matrix. It transforms a point p with row vectors as follows: p' = p * M * R + t. The scale/shear matrix M applies first, then the rotation R, then the translation t. The name follows the order of operations from right to left, as VQV does.

VQM keeps the advantages of VQV: the rotation stays a normalized quaternion, and the translation and the rotation interpolate separately. Unlike VQV, VQM forms a group: the multiplication and the inverse do not discard information, and the multiplication is associative. When a multiplication rotates a non-uniform scale, the result contains shear. VQV discards that shear, but VQM keeps it in M. The scale/shear matrix can also contain a negative scale and a reflection.

  • vqm_from_matrix finds the rotation with the Gram-Schmidt process. More than one VQM gives the same matrix: the function returns the one with a pure rotation, and M contains the reflection, if any.
  • vqm_get_scale returns the diagonal of M. vqm_get_scale_shear returns the full matrix.
  • vqm_lerp interpolates M with a linear interpolation. vqm_slerp interpolates the scale (the diagonal of M) with an exponential interpolation (vector_eerp) and the remaining shear with a linear interpolation.
  • vqm_inverse has a variant with a fallback scale for a scale/shear part that is not invertible.

A VQM uses four SIMD registers: 16 components, or 64 bytes for vqmf. When the scale/shear part is exactly the identity, the transform holds a flag. Then vqm_mul, vqm_mul_point3, vqm_mul_vector3, vqm_inverse, vqm_lerp, and vqm_slerp skip the scale/shear part and use only the rotation and the translation. With a scale/shear part, a VQM costs more than a VQV because the multiplication computes three 3x3 matrix products.

Include rtm/vqmf.h or rtm/vqmd.h.

For the theory, see The VQM-Group and its Applications by Michael Aristidou and Xin Li.

docs.title: Matrix 3x3
docs.text: A generic 3x3 matrix. Suitable to represent rotations mixed with 3D scale or anything else that might fit.

docs.title: Matrix 3x4
docs.text: An 3x4 affine matrix represents a 3D rotation, 3D translation, and 3D scale. It properly deals with skew/shear when present but once scale with mirroring is combined, it cannot be safely extracted back. Affine matrices are 4x4 but have their last row always equal to [0, 0, 0, 1] which is why it is named 3x4.

docs.title: Matrix 4x4
docs.text: A generic 4x4 matrix. Suitable to represent 3D projection matrices and the likes.

docs.title: Unaligned and storage friendly types
docs.text: When manipulating vectors of various width, it is often desirable to store them as an unaligned sequence of floats with no padding. For example, while a 3D mesh has a number of float3 vertices, storing and manipulating them as vector4f would use 33% more memory. To that end, a number of types are provided to help with this: float2f, float2d, float3f, float3d, float4f, float4d. These types have no alignment requirement beyond the natural float/double alignment. Functions such as vector_load3(const float3f* input) can load them from memory and return a vector4 of the correct type.

docs.title: matrix_look_to
docs.text:
matrix3x4d matrix_look_to(vector4d position, vector4d direction, vector4d up)

Returns a left-handed affine 3x4 matrix representing a camera transform. A camera transform multiplied by a point3 transforms a point3 local to the camera into world space. The camera transform is located at the specified position, looking towards the specified direction, and using the specified up direction.

The look to direction and up inputs do not need to be normalized.

In this frame of reference:

  • X axis: right direction
  • Y axis: up direction
  • Z axis: forward/look direction

docs.title: view_look_to
docs.text:
matrix3x4d view_look_to(vector4d position, vector4d direction, vector4d up)

Returns a left-handed affine 3x4 matrix representing a camera view transform. A camera view transform is the inverse of a camera transform. A camera transform multiplied by a point3 transforms a point3 local to the camera into world space while a camera view transform multiplied by a point3 does the opposite: it transforms a world space point3 into local space of the camera. This is typically used before applying a projection matrix. The camera transform is located at the specified position, looking towards the specified direction, and using the specified up direction. The camera view transform is then constructed from its inverse.

The look to direction and up inputs do not need to be normalized.

In this frame of reference:

  • X axis: right direction
  • Y axis: up direction
  • Z axis: forward/look direction

docs.text:
matrix3x3d matrix_transpose(matrix3x4d input)

Transposes a 3x4 affine matrix. Note: This transposes the upper 3x3 rotation/scale part of the matrix and it discards the translation. This is because a transposed 4x4 affine matrix is no longer affine due to its last row no longer being [0, 0, 0, 1]. The most common usage of an affine transpose operation is to construct the inverse transpose used to transform normal bi-vectors.

Transposes a 3x4 affine matrix. Note: This transposes the upper 3x3 rotation/scale part of the matrix and it discards the translation. docs.title: quat_lerp
docs.text:
quatd quat_lerp(quatd start, quatd end, double alpha)

Returns the linear interpolation between start and end for a given alpha value. The formula used is: ((1.0 - alpha) * start) + (alpha * end). Interpolation is stable and will return 'start' when 'alpha' is 0.0 and 'end' when it is 1.0. This is the same instruction count when FMA is present but it might be slightly slower due to the extra multiplication compared to: start + (alpha * (end - start)). Note that if 'start' and 'end' are on the opposite ends of the hypersphere, 'end' is negated before we interpolate. As such, when 'alpha' is 1.0, either 'end' or its negated equivalent is returned. Furthermore, if 'start' and 'end' aren't exactly normalized, the result might not match exactly when 'alpha' is 0.0 or 1.0 because we normalize the resulting quaternion.

docs.title: quat_slerp
docs.text:
quatd quat_slerp(quatd start, quatd end, double alpha)

Returns the spherical interpolation between start and end for a given alpha value. If the angle between the two inputs is near zero, the function uses the weights (1.0 - alpha) and alpha. See: https://www.euclideanspace.com/maths/algebra/realNormedAlgebra/quaternions/slerp/index.htm Perhaps try this someday: http://number-none.com/product/Understanding%20Slerp,%20Then%20Not%20Using%20It/

Returns a normalized quaternion using a deterministic algorithm. This ensures that for a given input, the output will be identical on all platforms that implement IEEE-754. This can be slower than quat_normalize. This is only guaranteed if the rounding modes are consistent. docs.title: quat_lerp
docs.text:
quatf quat_lerp(quatf start, quatf end, float alpha)

Returns the linear interpolation between start and end for a given alpha value. The formula used is: ((1.0 - alpha) * start) + (alpha * end). Interpolation is stable and will return 'start' when 'alpha' is 0.0 and 'end' when it is 1.0. This is the same instruction count when FMA is present but it might be slightly slower due to the extra multiplication compared to: start + (alpha * (end - start)). Note that if 'start' and 'end' are on the opposite ends of the hypersphere, 'end' is negated before we interpolate. As such, when 'alpha' is 1.0, either 'end' or its negated equivalent is returned. Furthermore, if 'start' and 'end' aren't exactly normalized, the result might not match exactly when 'alpha' is 0.0 or 1.0 because we normalize the resulting quaternion.

docs.title: quat_slerp
docs.text:
quatf quat_slerp(quatf start, quatf end, float alpha)

Returns the spherical interpolation between start and end for a given alpha value. If the angle between the two inputs is near zero, the function uses the weights (1.0 - alpha) and alpha. See: https://www.euclideanspace.com/maths/algebra/realNormedAlgebra/quaternions/slerp/index.htm Perhaps try this someday: http://number-none.com/product/Understanding%20Slerp,%20Then%20Not%20Using%20It/

Interpolation is stable and will return 'start' when alpha is 0.0 and 'end' when it is 1.0. Use it to interpolate a scale. The result is 'start' when alpha is 0.0. It is approximately 'end' when alpha is 1.0. The two inputs must have the same sign and must not be zero. docs.title: scalarf
docs.text:
A SIMD friendly scalar type. Different architectures have an easier or harder time working with scalar floating point numbers. For example, older PowerPC processors had to write to memory and reload from it to transfer from one register file into another (e.g convert from a float to a SIMD vector). Modern processors handle this much better but inefficiencies remain, especially with SSE. While it is free to convert a SIMD scalar into a float with _mm_cvtss_f32(..) the reverse generally requires the compiler to fill the unused SIMD lanes with known values (either zero or the same). This introduces an extra instruction that isn't always required when only the first lane is used such as with scalar_sqrt_reciprocal(..). By introducing a type for SIMD scalar values, each platform is free to make an optimal choice.

The definition of this type depends on the SIMD code path. Use the functions of RTM to read and write its values.

docs.text:
struct vqmf
{
    quatf rotation; // The rotation part.
    vector4f translation_m22; // The translation part in [xyz] and the m22 value of the scale/shear matrix in [w].
    vector4f x_axis_m20; // The X axis of the scale/shear matrix in [xyz] and the m20 value of that matrix in [w].
    vector4f y_axis_m21; // The Y axis of the scale/shear matrix in [xyz] and the m21 value of that matrix in [w].
};

A VQM transform represents a 3D rotation (quaternion), a 3D translation (vector), and a 3D scale/shear (3x3 matrix). The scale/shear part can contain a non-uniform scale, shear, and a reflection. A point transforms as follows: p' = p * M * R + t, with M the scale/shear matrix and R the rotation matrix of the quaternion. VQM transforms form a group: the multiplication and the inverse are well defined. The multiplication is associative but not commutative, as with quaternions and matrices. The rotation must be a normalized quaternion. The internal format is opaque: use the vqm_* functions. The [w] lanes hold the third row of M: m20 = z_axis.x, m21 = z_axis.y, and m22 = z_axis.z. Thus the transform uses 4 registers.

docs.text:
vector4d vector_lerp(vector4d start, vector4d end, double alpha)
vector4d vector_lerp(vector4d start, vector4d end, vector4d alpha)

Per component linear interpolation of the two inputs at the specified alpha. The formula used is: ((1.0 - alpha) * start) + (alpha * end). Interpolation is stable and will return 'start' when alpha is 0.0 and 'end' when it is 1.0. This is the same instruction count when FMA is present but it might be slightly slower due to the extra multiplication compared to: start + (alpha * (end - start)).

docs.title: vector_eerp
docs.text:
vector4d vector_eerp(vector4d start, vector4d end, double alpha)
vector4d vector_eerp(vector4d start, vector4d end, vector4d alpha)

Per component exponential interpolation of the two inputs at the specified alpha. The formula used is: start * (end / start)^alpha. For equal steps of alpha, the result changes by the same ratio. Use it to interpolate a scale. The result is 'start' when alpha is 0.0. It is approximately 'end' when alpha is 1.0. The two inputs must have the same sign and must not be zero. Otherwise, the result is undefined.

docs.text:
vector4f vector_lerp(vector4f start, vector4f end, float alpha)
vector4f vector_lerp(vector4f start, vector4f end, vector4f alpha)

Per component linear interpolation of the two inputs at the specified alpha. The formula used is: ((1.0 - alpha) * start) + (alpha * end). Interpolation is stable and will return 'start' when alpha is 0.0 and 'end' when it is 1.0. This is the same instruction count when FMA is present but it might be slightly slower due to the extra multiplication compared to: start + (alpha * (end - start)).

Per component linear interpolation of the two inputs at the specified alpha. The function interpolates the rotation with quat_lerp(..). It interpolates the translation and each axis of the scale/shear part with vector_lerp(..). The formula used is: ((1.0 - alpha) * start) + (alpha * end).

docs.title: vqm_slerp
docs.text:
vqmf vqm_slerp(vqmf start, vqmf end, float alpha)

Spherical interpolation of the two inputs at the specified alpha. The function interpolates the rotation with quat_slerp(..) and the translation with vector_lerp(..). The scale is the diagonal of the scale/shear part. The function interpolates the scale with vector_eerp(..) and the remaining shear with vector_lerp(..). If the two values of a scale have a different sign or if one value is zero, the function interpolates that lane of the rows of the scale/shear part with vector_lerp(..).

#include "rtm/vqvd.h"

WARNING: VQV transforms do NOT form a group. It has no well defined multiplication and inverse. This is because when non-uniform scale is rotated (e.g. as the result of two VQV multiplying), shear is introduced and there is no place to store it.
